summary: A 1970 note by E. Meyer pointing out an error in the Logger Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone spotted a mistake in the login rules and wrote it down.

subtitle: A notice pointing out a contradiction between two protocol specifications.

tldr.problem: A conflict was discovered between the official NCP protocol and the logger protocol, regarding when the ALL (allocate) command could be issued during connection setup.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC author points out that RFC 66 proposed sending an ALL command after an RTS or STR request, but the official protocol document only allowed ALL for already-open connections, creating incompatibility.
tldr.outcome: The logger protocol was modified to align with the existing NCP protocol rather than changing the core protocol, demonstrating a preference for stability over individual feature proposals.

today: RFC 79 is an Internet Experiment document. It is an early example of protocol conflict resolution in the ARPA network, illustrating the principle of favoring stability and compatibility over feature adoption during the experimental phase.

sections.title: The Protocol Conflict
sections.content:
RFC 79 documents a protocol conflict discovered by E. Meyer of MIT Project MAC. The conflict exists between the official NCP protocol as defined in Protocol Document 1 and the logger protocol proposed in RFC 66 by Steve Crocker.

According to RFC 66, an ALL (allocate) command should be sent immediately following an RTS (request to send) or STR (send-to-receive) request for connection. However, Protocol Document 1 restricts ALL commands to only be issued for connections that are already open, not during the connection setup phase.
sections.plainLanguage: One protocol said you could do action X at point A in the process, but another protocol said you could only do it at point B after the connection was already working.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content: This is not a trivial difference. The restriction that ALL can only be used on open connections is described as a simplifying constraint that NCP implementations could take advantage of. For example, the Multics NCP was already designed with this restriction in mind. Changing the core protocol to allow ALL before connections are open would require redesigning Multics and potentially other implementations already under development.
sections.plainLanguage: Some systems were already being built with the assumption that you couldn't do this during setup, so changing it would break their work.

sections.title: Decision and Impact
sections.content: The RFC concludes that the logger protocol should be modified to agree with the existing NCP protocol rather than changing the core protocol. The rationale was to avoid disrupting implementations already in progress and because the authors believed that the NCP protocol should not be changed except for critical reasons. This decision prioritized stability and compatibility over adopting the new feature proposed in RFC 66.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than make everyone redesign their systems, they decided to change the logger protocol to match what people were already building.
